summary: Barry Zhang, a member of technical staff on Anthropic's Applied AI team, shares practical learnings from building agentic systems with enterprises and startups, drawing on a blog post co-authored with Eric titled 'Building Effective Agents.' The talk is organized around three core ideas plus personal musings. First, agents should not be built for everything. Agents scale complex, valuable tasks but are not a drop-in upgrade. A checklist guides when to build agents: task complexity (agents thrive in ambiguous problem spaces), task value (exploration costs many tokens), derisking critical capabilities (no bottlenecks in trajectory), and cost of error and error discovery. Coding is highlighted as an ideal use case due to ambiguity, high value, proven model capability, and verifiable output via unit tests and CI. Second, agent architecture should be kept simple. Agents are defined as models using tools in a loop with three components: the environment, a set of tools, and a system prompt. Upfront complexity kills iteration speed. Three different agent use cases with different product surfaces share almost exactly the same backbone and code. Optimizations like trajectory caching, parallel tool calls, and progress presentation come only after basic behavior is established. Third, builders should think like their agents by putting themselves in the agent's context window. At each step, the model runs inference on only 10-20k tokens. A computer use agent example demonstrates this: the agent sees only static screenshots and brief descriptions, effectively operating with eyes closed for 3-5 seconds between actions. He also suggests using Claude itself to evaluate prompts, tool descriptions, and trajectories. He concludes with personal musings on three future directions: making agents budget-aware with better control over cost and latency, self-evolving tools where agents design and improve their own tool ergonomics making them more general purpose, and multi-agent collaboration in production by end of 2025, noting sub-agents can protect the main agent's context window and flagging asynchronous inter-agent communication as a key open question. He closes with an anecdote about claiming the inaugural 'AI Engineer' title at Meta in 2023 after reading Swix's blog post, motivated by making AI practically useful.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Three Core Ideas
sections.summary: Barry introduces himself and the talk's structure around three core ideas from the 'Building Effective Agents' blog post: don't build agents for everything, keep it simple, and think like your agents, plus personal musings at the end.

sections.title: Evolution of Agentic Systems
sections.summary: Traces the progression from simple features like summarization and classification, to workflows with predefined control flows trading cost and latency for performance, to domain-specific agents that decide their own trajectory based on environment feedback. Notes that as agency increases, cost, latency, and error consequences also rise.

sections.title: Don't Build Agents for Everything
sections.summary: Presents a checklist for when to build agents: task complexity (agents thrive in ambiguity), task value (must justify token cost), derisking critical capabilities (no bottlenecks), and cost of error and error discovery. Uses coding as an ideal example due to ambiguity, value, proven capability, and verifiable output via unit tests and CI.

sections.title: Keep It Simple
sections.summary: Defines agents as models using tools in a loop with three components: environment, tools, and system prompt. Emphasizes that upfront complexity kills iteration speed. Three different agent use cases share nearly identical backbone code. Optimizations like trajectory caching, parallel tool calls, and progress presentation come after basic behavior is established.

sections.title: Think Like Your Agents
sections.summary: Recommends putting yourself in the agent's context window: at each step the model only sees 10-20k tokens. Demonstrates with a computer use agent example showing the agent sees only static screenshots and brief descriptions, effectively blind for 3-5 seconds between actions. Suggests using Claude to audit prompts, tool descriptions, and trajectories.

sections.title: Personal Musings: Budget-Aware Agents, Self-Evolving Tools, and Multi-Agent Collaboration
sections.summary: Introduces three future directions. First: making agents budget-aware with better control over cost and latency, with open questions about defining and enforcing budgets in time, money, and tokens. Second: self-evolving tools, where agents can design and improve their own tool ergonomics, making them more general purpose. Third: multi-agent collaboration in production by end of 2025, with well-parallelized systems, nice separation of concerns, and sub-agents protecting the main agent's context window. Key open question: how agents communicate with each other, given current systems are built around rigid synchronous user-assistant turns; asynchronous communication and expanded roles are needed.

sections.title: Conclusion and Personal Anecdote
sections.summary: Recaps three takeaways: don't build agents for everything, keep it simple, and think like your agent. Shares socials for continued conversation. Closes with a personal anecdote about changing his job description to 'AI Engineer' at Meta in 2023 after reading Swix's blog post, motivated by the focus on practicality and making AI useful to the world.
